title: Pollard's rho, worked on a small curve
one_liner: One walk followed step by step until it repeats and gives up the key, then two thousand more measured against the prediction for a random function.
index_meta: Worked example · a curve with {{n}} points
description: Pollard's rho method run on a small elliptic curve: the walk, the collision that reveals the discrete logarithm, the rho shape drawn to scale, and measured walk lengths for Pollard's original walk and Teske's r-adding walk.
standfirst: The attack page gives the idea and the cost. This page runs it: on a curve with {{n}} points it follows one walk until it repeats, recovers the key from the repeat, and then measures how long such walks take on average.

facts.This walk: {{steps}} steps to its first repeated point; √n ≈ {{sqrt_n}}
facts.Measured over {{trials}} walks each: Pollard's original walk {{pollard_S}}√n, a {{teske_r}}-adding walk {{teske_S}}√n; a random function would take {{predicted_S}}√n

blocks.p: The curve is y2 = x3 + {{a}}x + {{b}} over F{{p}}. It has {{n}} points, and since that number is prime every point other than O generates the whole group, so there is no smaller subgroup for Pohlig–Hellman to exploit. Rho is the right tool, and for a random walk on {{n}} points the birthday bound predicts a repeat after about √(πn/2) ≈ {{expected_steps}} steps.
Take P = {{P}}. The code that builds this page picks a secret k at random and publishes Q = kP = {{Q}}. The walk below never sees k; it only adds points and compares them.

Each point the walk visits is written as a known combination X<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>P + b<sub>i</sub>Q. Pollard's original rule looks at the x-coordinate modulo 3 and makes one of three moves, updating the coefficients to match:

ul: x ≡ 0: add P, so a increases by 1;
x ≡ 1: double, so a and b both double;
x ≡ 2: add Q, so b increases by 1.

blocks.p: The rule depends only on the current point, so once the walk reaches a point it has seen before, it repeats everything that followed. Start from random a<sub>0</sub> and b<sub>0</sub>:
At step {{j}} the walk returns to {{Xi}}, which it first reached at step {{i}}. That one point now has two representations:

blocks.label: Subtracting the two representations of X<sub>{{i}}</sub> = X<sub>{{j}}</sub>.
Dividing is possible because n is prime and b<sub>{{i}}</sub> ≠ b<sub>{{j}}</sub>. The build checks that {{recovered}}P = Q.

blocks.p: This walk took {{steps}} steps, {{ratio}}√n, against the {{expected_steps}} the birthday bound suggests. One walk is one sample; the next section measures the average.

The code behind this page keeps every visited point in a table, which is the clearest way to show where the repeat happens and costs nothing at this size. At 2128 steps it is impossible. Floyd's and Brent's cycle-finding methods detect the repeat while storing only a couple of points. Parallel implementations instead report only distinguished points, those whose x-coordinate starts with a fixed number of zero bits, to a central server: two walks that merge reach the same distinguished point, the server sees it twice, and the logarithm follows exactly as above. That is the van Oorschot–Wiener method described on the attack page.

The {{expected_steps}}-step prediction assumes the walk behaves like a random function. Whether it does is a property of the rule, and it can be measured. For each of two rules the code ran {{trials}} walks, each with a fresh random target and starting point, and counted the steps until the first repeated point.

Pollard's original rule is measurably worse than random: its walks run {{pollard_excess}}% longer. Teske identified the problem and proposed r-adding walks, which add one of r fixed random combinations of P and Q chosen by the current point. With r = {{teske_r}} the measured mean is {{teske_S}}, {{teske_excess}}% from the random-function value. A heuristic due to Brent and Pollard says an r-adding walk should be slower than random by a factor of 1/√(1 − 1/r), {{teske_penalty}}% for r = {{teske_r}}, and the measurement agrees with it to within its standard error.
This ratio, operations divided by √n, is the number our discrete-log library reports for every solver, so that different algorithms and implementations can be compared directly.

Nothing in the walk changes for a 256-bit curve except the numbers. The rule, the coefficients and the final division are the same. What changes is that √(πn/4) is about 2127.8, which no computation will reach; the table of standard curves is in the note on the ECDLP. In the other direction, a 60-bit group needs only about 230 steps, well within one computer's reach, and the public records sit between those extremes, near 114 bits.
